outputs.L1:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Wearing a plaid green A-line spring skirt from her new fashion line, cinched with a black patent leather belt and paired with black leather gladiator stiletto sandals, “Sex and the City” actress Kristin Davis is the perfect blend of sweet and fierce when we meet after her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia.

Davis is surrounded by models and Belk store official Arlene Goldstein. Her look is pure Charlotte, with just a touch of her on-screen friend Carrie.

Davis is so much like her character—adorable and upbeat—that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to drop into our conversation and say something shocking.

As any true fan knows—OK, as every woman knows—watching “Sex and the City” was like sitting in the front row at a fashion show with a plot. Costume designer Patricia Field dressed the television and movie characters in haute couture as they skipped through the streets of New York City in $600 stilettos.

But is that reality? Most sane women would not choose to walk even one city block in high heels. And most certainly cannot spend a month’s rent on a belt or bag, even if they have a truly fabulous party at which to wear it.

So what about the fashionistas on a budget? Are we to be ignored, forced to wear boring clothes and practical shoes?

Luckily, no. Designers are catching on. Target features affordable collections from high-end designers such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Every piece in Sarah Jessica Parker’s clothing line, Bitten, cost less than $20 before the store that carried it went under.

Davis is the latest celebrity to jump on the clothing-label bandwagon, designing a line for Belk department stores. Will she meet the same fate as Parker?

Davis has the following to succeed. Although her character was by far the most conservatively dressed—Carrie strolling through town in only a bra top, anyone?—Charlotte had the most wearable wardrobe. Along with the rest of the show’s leading ladies, Davis became a fashion icon.

Her favorite piece from the collection?

“I can’t decide, impossible to choose!” she says.

So I choose for her: definitely the gladiator heels.

“It’s important for women to have a strong shoe,” she says. “Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you’re good to go.”

Davis admits that she did not have a defined style before meeting Field, who bluntly told her that “Sexy Secretary” was going to be her look.

Davis’ philosophy is a sound one: Stick with what works. She draws on the look Field created for her “Sex and the City” character. Original it may not be, but everything coming down the runway is something the stylish Charlotte York would undoubtedly wear.

Davis is also in touch with real women.

“I don’t want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear,” she says.

Her solution? Dresses, shoes and swimsuits worthy of a “Sex and the City” episode—without requiring Park Avenue pockets to afford them. The collection is versatile enough to flatter every body type.

“Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!” she says with a laugh.

Davis will not reveal any secrets from the script of the “Sex and the City” movie sequel, due out in May 2010, but she does say it is a “happy” movie. She also hints that, as art imitates life, our famous foursome may have to cut back a little on their clothing expenses.

She is, however, willing to share some fashion advice. How can you look as though you have just stepped out of the wardrobe room on the set of the next “Sex and the City” movie?

Green.

“It’s THE color,” she says.

And, hey, who does not need to save some green? It all works out perfectly.

After meeting Davis, I went to see her displays. Then I skipped into the streets of Atlanta in a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals—which, of course, I bought on sale.
outputs.L2:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — When I catch up with “Sex and the City” star Kristin Davis following her fashion show at Atlanta’s Belk department store, she is dressed in a green plaid A-line spring skirt from her newly launched collection. A black patent-leather belt and towering black leather gladiator sandals complete an outfit that manages to appear both charming and bold. Nearby, Davis poses with models and Belk representative Arlene Goldstein.

The ensemble feels mostly Charlotte, Davis’ television character, with a hint of her on-screen friend Carrie. In person, Davis is so cheerful and endearing—much like Charlotte—that it seems entirely possible Carrie or Samantha could suddenly join us and say something outrageous enough to make her blush.

For devoted viewers—or really, for virtually any woman—“Sex and the City” offered a fashion show woven into a storyline. Patricia Field, who designed the costumes for both the television series and the movie, sent the characters through New York City in couture clothing and stilettos costing $600.

Of course, that fantasy bears little resemblance to everyday life. Few sensible women would willingly walk even a single city block in very high heels, and most cannot devote the equivalent of a month’s rent to a handbag or belt, no matter how spectacular the event they plan to attend.

Does that mean style-conscious women with limited budgets must settle for dull clothes and sensible footwear? Fortunately, designers and retailers have begun recognizing that market. Target, for example, has offered lower-priced collections by luxury designers including Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Every item in Sarah Jessica Parker’s Bitten clothing brand was priced below $20, although the retailer selling the collection later went out of business.

Now Davis has joined the growing list of celebrities with fashion labels by creating a collection for Belk. Could her venture end the way Parker’s did? Davis appears to have an audience that could help make it succeed. Charlotte was easily the most modest dresser among the show’s characters—unlike Carrie, who once walked around the city wearing only a bra top—but her closet was also the easiest for ordinary women to imagine wearing. Like her co-stars, Davis ultimately became a fashion icon.

Asked to name the item she likes best in her collection, Davis refuses to pick, declaring that deciding is impossible. I make the choice for her: the gladiator heels.

Women need footwear that makes a statement, she explains. Once the shoes are strong, almost anything can be worn above them, and the outfit is ready.

Before working with Field, Davis says she did not have a clearly established personal style. Field changed that by directly announcing that Davis’ image would be “Sexy Secretary.”

Davis has since adopted a practical approach: continue with a formula that has already proved successful. Her collection draws heavily on the aesthetic Field created for Charlotte in “Sex and the City.” The idea may not be especially new, but every runway outfit looks like something the fashionable Charlotte York would happily choose.

At the same time, Davis says she is thinking about women outside Hollywood. She has no interest in producing clothes that look right only on very thin actresses. Instead, she offers dresses, bathing suits and shoes glamorous enough for a “Sex and the City” episode but affordable without a Park Avenue-size bank account. The pieces are intended to flatter a range of figures.

Everyone worries about some aspect of her body, Davis says, so she wanted to design clothes that would suit many different shapes. To test that goal, she even recruited members of her family to try on the garments, she adds with a laugh.

Davis will not reveal anything confidential about the script for the “Sex and the City” movie sequel, scheduled for release in May 2010. She does, however, describe the film as happy and suggests that, with fiction reflecting real economic conditions, the famous group of four friends may need to reduce their fashion spending somewhat.

She is more forthcoming with style advice. For anyone who wants to look as though she has just emerged from the wardrobe department of the next “Sex and the City” film, Davis recommends green, calling it the essential color.

And since everyone could benefit from saving a little “green” as well, the theme comes together neatly.

After leaving Davis, I examine the displays of her collection. Then I head onto the streets of Atlanta wearing a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals—which, naturally, I purchased on sale.

# Kristin Davis brings accessible glamour to Belk with an affordable clothing line

**ATLANTA** — Kristin Davis may be forever associated with Charlotte York’s polished Park Avenue wardrobe, but the actress is taking a more down-to-earth approach to fashion with an affordable clothing collection for Belk.

Unveiled at the department store’s Atlanta location, the line blends feminine dresses, tailored separates and easy knitwear with the refined aesthetic Davis made famous on HBO’s “Sex and the City.” The difference is that these pieces are intended for everyday closets — and everyday budgets.

“Fashion should make women feel welcome, not judged,” Davis said at the launch. “I wanted to create clothes for different bodies and different stages of life, because style shouldn’t belong to only one size or shape.”

The collection leans into Davis’ signature romanticism, with flattering waistlines, soft colors and classic prints. But it also includes practical staples designed to move from work to dinner without requiring a costume change.

Davis said her own style is less rigid than Charlotte’s carefully coordinated wardrobe, though the character’s influence remains unmistakable.

“My ‘Sex and the City’ style will always be part of me,” she said. “I love beautiful dresses and feminine details, but in real life I also want clothes that are comfortable and easy to wear.”

Accessories provide a bolder counterpoint to the collection’s softer silhouettes. Davis said she prefers footwear that feels grounded rather than fragile.

“I like strong shoes,” she said. “Even with a very feminine dress, I want a shoe that has presence — something you can actually walk in and feel confident wearing.”

That balance of glamour and practicality is central to the partnership with Belk, whose customers Davis described as women looking for fashion that fits into full, busy lives. By keeping prices accessible, she hopes shoppers can experiment without treating every purchase as an investment-piece decision.

The Atlanta launch drew fans eager for both a glimpse of Davis and a little of the elegance associated with “Sex and the City.” Yet Davis emphasized that the collection is not about dressing like Charlotte. It is about helping women find their own version of confidence.

“The best style is the style that lets you feel like yourself,” she said. “If a dress makes you stand taller and smile when you look in the mirror, then it’s doing its job.”

### Kristin Davis Brings Charlotte York Polish to the People

Fresh from presenting her new fashion collection in Atlanta, Kristin Davis looked less like an actress dabbling in design than a woman who knows exactly what her audience wants: pretty dresses, flattering silhouettes and a little Park Avenue fantasy at an attainable price.

The budget-friendly line translates Davis’s famously feminine image into wearable pieces—fit-and-flare dresses, tidy knits, polished separates and romantic details that can move from office hours to dinner reservations. Inevitably, the collection evokes Charlotte York, Davis’s impeccably mannered *Sex and the City* character, whose wardrobe favored cinched waists, graceful skirts and clothes that always appeared properly introduced.

But there is more wink than primness here. The collection also recalls costume designer Patricia Field’s “Sexy Secretary” approach to Charlotte: conservative codes sharpened with body-conscious tailoring, a strategic neckline or a pair of formidable heels. The appeal lies in that tension. A cardigan may be sweet, but it is never sleepy; a classic dress may look luncheon-ready, yet still understands cocktail hour.

Davis makes a natural ambassador for this kind of accessible glamour. Her style has never depended on fashion-world intimidation. Instead, she sells polish as a pleasure—something achievable without Charlotte’s Upper East Side budget or closet space.

After Atlanta, the message was clear: this is not Carrie Bradshaw’s high-risk fashion laboratory or Samantha Jones’s seduction uniform. It is Charlotte’s world, loosened up, priced down and offered with Davis’s warm, self-aware charm. The result is ladylike dressing with a pulse—the “Sexy Secretary” clocking out early and heading somewhere far more interesting.

# Charlotte Style, Minus the Park Avenue Price Tag

For *Sex and the City* fans, Kristin Davis will always be Charlotte York: polished, romantic and rarely seen without an immaculate dress and an enviable pair of heels. But achieving Charlotte’s Upper East Side look no longer requires a trust fund—or a closet full of couture.

Davis brought her ladylike aesthetic to Belk with an accessible collection of dresses, separates, shoes, handbags and jewelry. The line translates Charlotte’s signature refinement into practical pieces: feminine prints, defined waists, classic silhouettes and enough color to keep the look from feeling overly conservative.

## Uptown Polish at Department-Store Prices

The smartest pieces in the Kristin Davis collection are also the most versatile. A fitted dress can go from the office to cocktails with a change of accessories, while a soft blouse or tailored cardigan adds instant polish to jeans. Look for details that feel expensive without being fussy: flattering necklines, subtle ruching, fabric-covered belts and saturated jewel tones.

The key is not to copy Charlotte costume for costume. Instead, borrow her formula:

- Choose one beautifully shaped piece as the foundation.
- Emphasize the waist.
- Keep prints feminine and accessories coordinated.
- Finish with a structured bag and a confident shoe.

The result is Park Avenue-inspired rather than Park Avenue-priced.

## Step Into Gladiator Heels

For shoppers whose style leans more Carrie than Charlotte, gladiator heels provide the necessary dose of fashion drama. The strappy sandals remain a strong choice because they can toughen up even the sweetest dress.

Wear metallic or neutral gladiators with a floral frock to prevent the outfit from looking too precious. Black versions work well with a simple sheath or cropped trousers, while lower, sturdier heels offer the same trend-conscious effect without requiring Carrie Bradshaw’s tolerance for pain.

A word of caution: ankle straps visually divide the leg. Petite shoppers may prefer nude-toned straps or a more open design, while those with athletic calves can look for styles that sit lower on the ankle rather than wrapping upward. And if the shoe is elaborate, let it be the star—skip the oversized handbag, statement necklace and cocktail ring all at once.

## Dress for Your Shape, Not a Character’s

The best lesson from *Sex and the City* is not that every woman needs designer labels. It is that personal style works best when it celebrates the wearer.

**For hourglass figures:**  
Try wrap dresses, belted sheaths and fit-and-flare silhouettes. Defined waists echo Davis’ feminine aesthetic without adding bulk.

**For pear-shaped figures:**  
Choose dresses with detail near the neckline or shoulders, then keep the skirt fluid rather than clingy. A-line shapes create balance, and darker bottoms paired with brighter tops draw the eye upward.

**For apple-shaped figures:**  
Look for V-necks, softly structured jackets and dresses with strategic ruching. An empire or slightly raised waist can provide shape without squeezing the midsection.

**For straight or athletic figures:**  
Create curves with peplum-like details, full skirts, draping and belts. Prints and textured fabrics can also add dimension.

**For petite frames:**  
Keep proportions neat. A knee-length dress, cropped cardigan and streamlined heel will usually be more flattering than an oversized print or ankle-swallowing straps.

**For tall or fuller figures:**  
Take advantage of bold color, larger prints and longer lines. A well-fitted garment is more flattering than one chosen simply because it is loose; tailoring remains the quickest route to a luxurious look.

## Will Charlotte Return in 2010?

The fashion conversation is likely to get another boost in 2010. A second *Sex and the City* movie is in the works, with Sarah Jessica Parker, Kristin Davis, Kim Cattrall and Cynthia Nixon expected to return as Carrie, Charlotte, Samantha and Miranda.

Story details are being kept under wraps, but the sequel is expected to revisit the friendships, marriages and romantic complications that made the first film a hit. For Charlotte fans, the most intriguing question may be how marriage and motherhood shape her wardrobe. Will she remain loyal to prim dresses, pearls and picture-perfect accessories—or will the sequel reveal a more relaxed side?

Whatever happens, one thing seems certain: the clothes will be treated as supporting characters. And with Davis’ Belk collection offering an affordable version of her refined style, fans will not have to wait for the movie—or max out a credit card—to dress the part.

# Kristin Davis Brings Charlotte-Inspired Style to Real Women—No Park Avenue Budget Required

Charlotte York’s polished wardrobe has always looked as if it came with a doorman, a trust fund and an ironclad no-wrinkles policy. Kristin Davis, however, is bringing that feminine, put-together spirit into the real world—with clothes women can actually wear and prices that don’t require a dramatic call to the bank.

The actress’s fashion offering channels Charlotte’s signature romanticism without turning into costume. Think flattering dresses rather than fussy frocks, pretty shoes designed for more than stepping out of a town car, and swimsuits made with actual bodies—and actual movement—in mind.

The dresses are the natural stars. They’re ladylike but approachable, with easy silhouettes, waist-defining shapes and enough polish for a wedding, dinner date or office day when you want everyone to wonder whether you have somewhere fabulous to go afterward. In other words: Upper East Side energy, everyday schedule.

Shoes follow the same formula. They’re feminine and refined, but not so precious that they must remain seated through an entire cocktail party. Paired with one of the collection’s dresses—or simply jeans and a crisp blouse—they offer a quick hit of Charlotte-style charm.

Then there’s swimwear, a category that can make even the most enthusiastic shopper suddenly develop urgent errands elsewhere. Davis’s approach is refreshingly wearable: flattering cuts, thoughtful coverage and glamour that doesn’t depend on standing perfectly still beside a pool. These are swimsuits for swimming, lounging, chasing children and ordering lunch without hiding behind a beach towel.

And expect plenty of green. The color is a Davis favorite, and it makes perfect sense here: emerald feels elegant, leaf green looks fresh, and softer shades provide an alternative to the endless sea of black. It’s cheerful, flattering and just bold enough to attract compliments without demanding a spotlight.

The best part? The pricing stays accessible. The collection delivers a taste of Charlotte’s polished world without requiring Charlotte’s fictional shopping allowance. That means real women can pick up a dress, add shoes—or even venture into swimwear—without treating the purchase like a major financial plotline.

Call it Charlotte-inspired, Kristin-approved and reality-ready: feminine fashion with a wink, a waistline and a price tag that understands we don’t all live on Park Avenue.
